faq.a: Yes, especially chronic HBV/HCV; routine labs often first clue.
They can worsen renal perfusion and increase bleeding risk in coagulopathy.
Only when non‑invasive scores are inconclusive or to stage fibrosis before therapy.

exam: What bedside findings differentiate acute viral hepatitis from cholestatic jaundice? — Look for marked transaminase rise, minimal ALP rise, tender hepatomegaly.
A patient with HBV presents with ALT 800 U/L, bilirubin 4 mg/dL, INR 1.6. What is the next step? — Admit, start antiviral therapy, monitor for encephalopathy.
Why is tenofovir preferred over lamivudine for chronic HBV in low‑resource settings? — Higher barrier to resistance, once‑daily dosing, good renal safety.
How would you assess fibrosis if FibroScan is unavailable? — Calculate APRI: (AST/ULN ÷ platelet × 100); >1.0 suggests significant fibrosis.
A pregnant woman with suspected HEV infection develops jaundice. What is the key concern? — High maternal mortality; monitor for fulminant liver failure.
What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral for a patient with chronic hepatitis C? — New onset encephalopathy or ascites indicating decompensation.
Explain why herbal remedies can cause hepatitis and how to counsel patients. — Many contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids causing centrilobular necrosis; advise avoidance and disclose safe alternatives.
When is liver transplantation indicated in acute severe hepatitis? — Persistent INR >2.0, encephalopathy grade III‑IV, and no improvement after 48‑72 h despite optimal care.
ai.title: Acute and Chronic Hepatitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hepatitis describes inflammation of the liver caused by viruses, toxins, or systemic disease. Acute hepatitis may resolve, while chronic hepatitis leads to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis.

b: Acute: symptom onset ≤6 weeks, ALT >5 × ULN, usually self‑limited.
Chronic: >6 months of abnormal liver tests or histologic inflammation.
sections.p: Inflammation of hepatic parenchyma confirmed by clinical features, liver enzyme pattern and, when possible, serology or imaging.

b: Mild: ALT <5 × ULN, bilirubin <2 mg/dL, INR <1.5.
Severe acute: ALT >10 × ULN, bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL, INR ≥1.5, encephalopathy.
Chronic fibrosis: F0‑F1 (no fibrosis) to F4 (cirrhosis).
sections.p: Severity is graded by transaminase level, bilirubin, INR and clinical decompensation; chronic disease is staged by fibrosis (METAVIR F0‑F4).

b: Viral: HBV, HCV, HAV (outbreaks), HEV (pregnancy).
Alcoholic liver disease.
Traditional herbal remedies (e.g., pyrrolizidine alkaloids).
Co‑existing HIV or TB treatment hepatotoxicity.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings viral hepatitis B and C dominate, followed by alcohol, herbal toxins, and co‑infection with HIV or malaria.

b: Jaundice: scleral icterus, yellow skin.
RUQ tenderness, hepatomegaly.
Dark urine, pale stools.
Ascites or peripheral edema in cirrhosis.
sections.p: Patients may have jaundice, right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort, nausea, and fatigue; acute cases often have fever and malaise, chronic disease is often silent until decompensation.
Select tests that answer the key clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there hepatocellular injury? Marked elevation (>5 × ULN) supports acute hepatitis.
Is cholestasis or severe liver dysfunction present? Bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL indicates significant dysfunction.
Is synthetic function impaired? INR ≥1.5 suggests severe disease or cirrhosis.

t.a: HBV surface antigen, anti‑HBc IgM, HCV antibody
t.b: Which viral cause? Positive HBsAg = chronic HBV; anti‑HBc IgM = acute HBV.
Is there fibrosis, steatosis, or biliary obstruction? Coarse echotexture supports chronic disease.

t.a: FibroScan or APRI score (when FibroScan unavailable)
t.b: What is fibrosis stage? APRI >1.0 suggests significant fibrosis.

b: Encephalopathy, INR ≥1.5, bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL.
Bleeding varices, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis.
sections.p: Identify patients at risk of rapid deterioration or long‑term sequelae.

b: Antiviral therapy for HBV (tenofovir/entecavir) or HCV (direct‑acting agents) when available.
Cessation of alcohol and hepatotoxic herbs.
N‑acetylcysteine for acute severe hepatitis (if acetaminophen suspected).
Vitamin K for coagulopathy, diuretics for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy.
Avoid NSAIDs and paracetamol >2 g/day in active hepatitis.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support liver function, and prevent complications.

b: ALT/AST, bilirubin, INR every 3‑6 months in chronic disease.
Ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months for cirrhosis surveillance.
HBV vaccination for contacts, safe injection practices.
Education on avoiding unsafe herbal remedies.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents progression and detects cancer early.

b: Gallstone cholangitis – presents with jaundice but has marked ALP elevation.
Leptospirosis – fever, jaundice, renal failure; requires serology.
Septicemia with DIC – high bilirubin but normal transaminases.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic hepatitis clinically or biochemically.

b: Mild ALT rise in early chronic HBV may be missed; rely on serology.
Bilirubin may be normal in early fibrosis; use fibrosis scores.
INR can be falsely normal if patient is on warfarin; assess clinical bleeding.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status, INR ≥1.5, bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL, massive ascites, or sudden haemorrhage.
